data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'conventionalist decision' to act as if the best-tested theory is true, accepting the cost that this preference offers no guarantee of future success or increased verisimilitude.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference implies a belief that the theory is more likely to be true.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the decision relies on any assumption of nature's uniformity beyond the logical possibility of falsification.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' is denied, specifically the lack of probabilistic justification for future performance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Methodological Conventionalism: The scientist adopts a rule of action (prefer the best-tested) not because it predicts truth, but because it is the most rational available strategy for error elimination, distinct from an inductive belief that the future will resemble the past.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
